description: At first I thought this was a different bird but I’m pretty sure this mallard is actually the same species as the ones next to it. Only difference between the two is the absence of color in the main duck photographed. His head is mostly black and white compared to the very green duck next to it. A lot of the ducks I’ve noticed seemed to very much vary in color heads and fur, which is very cool. I’ve seen some with green heads, blue heads, grey heads, and more. Considering they all look alike, move together, and the plaque describing the birds has them as one, I think they’re the same species. If not, then I wonder if they’d be so friendly outside of this confined lake. It’s possible the confinement of this place forced them to be as one, but most likely they’re just different colors.

Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) Males (drakes) have an iridescent green head and neck, yellow bill, narrow white collar, brown breast. Black central tail feathers curl up. Female (hens) have mottled plumage. Nesting sites are typically on the ground, hidden in vegetation where the female's speckled plumage serves as effective camouflage. Hen lays 8–13 creamy white eggs. Incubation takes 27 to 28 days and fledging takes 50 to 60 days. The ducklings are precocial and fully capable of swimming as soon as they hatch.
Feeding Behavior: forages in water by dabbling, submerging head and neck, up-ending, rarely by diving; forages on land by grazing, plucking seeds, grubbing for roots.

This is a picture of male and female Mallard ducks (Anas platyrhynchos) taken at a pond on Slippery Rock University. They are migratory waterfowl that are native to North America. The males have green iridescent heads, bright yellow beaks, a white collar, and brown, white and gray feathers on the body. The female is mostly brown and gray with an orange beak. Both have a bright blue strip on feathers on the back of their wings and orange webbed feet. They are omnivores that eat grasses, seeds, roots, stems, insects, crustaceans, amphibians, and small fish. They forage in the water by dabbling and will rarely dive. They have 5-10 eggs in a clutch and live upwards of 10 years.

description:
Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) Males (drakes) have an iridescent green head and neck, yellow bill, narrow white collar, brown breast. Black central tail feathers curl up. Female (hens) have mottled plumage. Nesting sites are typically on the ground, hidden in vegetation where the female's speckled plumage serves as effective camouflage. Hen lays 8–13 creamy white eggs. Incubation takes 27 to 28 days and fledging takes 50 to 60 days. The ducklings are precocial and fully capable of swimming as soon as they hatch.
Feeding Behavior: forages in water by dabbling, submerging head and neck, up-ending, rarely by diving; forages on land by grazing, plucking seeds, grubbing for roots.

description:
Male

Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) Males (drakes) have an iridescent green head and neck, yellow bill, narrow white collar, brown breast. Black central tail feathers curl up. Female (hens) have mottled plumage. Nesting sites are typically on the ground, hidden in vegetation where the female's speckled plumage serves as effective camouflage. Hen lays 8–13 creamy white eggs. Incubation takes 27 to 28 days and fledging takes 50 to 60 days. The ducklings are precocial and fully capable of swimming as soon as they hatch.
Feeding Behavior: forages in water by dabbling, submerging head and neck, up-ending, rarely by diving; forages on land by grazing, plucking seeds, grubbing for roots.

description:
Female

Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) Males (drakes) have an iridescent green head and neck, yellow bill, narrow white collar, brown breast. Black central tail feathers curl up. Female (hens) have mottled plumage. Nesting sites are typically on the ground, hidden in vegetation where the female's speckled plumage serves as effective camouflage. Hen lays 8–13 creamy white eggs. Incubation takes 27 to 28 days and fledging takes 50 to 60 days. The ducklings are precocial and fully capable of swimming as soon as they hatch.
Feeding Behavior: forages in water by dabbling, submerging head and neck, up-ending, rarely by diving; forages on land by grazing, plucking seeds, grubbing for roots.

Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) is an aquatic waterfowl in the Ducks, Geese, and Swans (Anatidae) family. "The Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) is a dabbling duck that breeds throughout the temperate and subtropical Americas, Eurasia, and North Africa. It has been introduced to New Zealand, Australia, Peru, Brazil, Uruguay, Argentina, Chile, Colombia, the Falkland Islands, and South Africa.
Breeding pairs look very different. Males (drakes) have an iridescent green head and neck, yellow bill, narrow white collar, brown breast. Black central tail feathers curl up. Female (hens) have mottled plumage. Mallards, like other ducks, shed all their flight feathers at the end of the breeding season and are flightless for 3–4 weeks. They are secretive during this vulnerable time, and their body feathers molt into a concealing “eclipse” plumage that can make them hard to identify.
Mallard pairs are generally monogamous, but paired males pursue females other than their mates. So-called “extra-pair copulations” are common among birds and in many species are consensual, but male Mallards often force these copulations, with several males chasing a single female and then mating with her. Mallard pairs form long before the spring breeding season. Pairing takes place in the fall, but courtship can be seen all winter. Only the female incubates the eggs and takes care of the ducklings. Nesting sites are typically on the ground, hidden in vegetation where the female's speckled plumage serves as effective camouflage. Hen lays 8–13 creamy white eggs. Incubation takes 27 to 28 days and fledging takes 50 to 60 days. The ducklings are precocial and fully capable of swimming as soon as they hatch. Mallards forage in water by dabbling, submerging head and neck, up-ending, but rarely by diving. It forages on land by grazing, plucking seeds, and grubbing for roots.
The standard duck’s quack is the sound of a female Mallard. Males don’t quack; they make a quieter, rasping sound." https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/6930-Anas-platyrhynchos

In my opinion this bird has too many Mallard genes and thus a hybrid. One concern with this bird is the slightly curled black upper tail coverts. Its face is dark and not gray. Many green flecks on the crown are seen at a certain angle. We were disturbed to see that the Mounds Pool 3 dike is closed for "environmentally sensitive" species; it would have been nice if there was signage at the Tower Pond parking lot to indicate this. We left at 1758 and drove to the lighthouse area.

Note 1: These records are exclusively from the Mounds Pool 3 dike to around the "closed" sign. Records from the Tower Pond Trail are kept separate. Because we were pressed for time, we reluctantly had to skip counting some shorebird species, and only estimated totals for some others (e.g., Blue-winged Teal).

A total of 7.
